title: Zero RLS backstop on the entire axhy schema — withTenantContext GUC is set but never enforced; one missing companyId filter = silent cross-tenant leak
where: apps/backend/src/middleware/tenant-context.ts:230-261 (withTenantContext sets axhy.current_company_id via SET LOCAL) vs prod pg_class/pg_policies
scenario: Defense-in-depth gap, not a current exploit. The code comment at tenant-context.ts:184-189 states RLS exists only on axhy_chat.turn_embeddings / axhy_graph / axhy_audit. I verified against prod: every table in the axhy schema (Worker, Visit, Assignment, LeaveRequest, SwapRequest, Complaint, ChatMessage, SupervisorDecision, Membership, etc.) has relrowsecurity=false and pg_policies returns [] for schemaname='axhy'. So the SET LOCAL axhy.current_company_id executed on every withTenantContext transaction is dead weight in the app schema — no policy reads it. The whole multi-tenant guarantee therefore depends on every one of ~167 findMany/findFirst/update calls manually including companyId. Today all of them do, but there is no second line of defense: a single future handler that forgets companyId (or a dynamic where-builder that conditionally drops it) leaks another tenant's rows with nothing to catch it.
evidence: Layer 1 (route claim): tenant-context.ts:4-6 + multiple route docblocks claim 'runs inside withTenantContext ... so RLS policies fire as a defense in depth' (e.g. complaints.ts:30-34). Layer 2 (route code): withTenantContext (tenant-context.ts:243-246) runs SELECT set_config('axhy.current_company_id',$1,true) then only a Company.status==ACTIVE check at :249-255; it does NOT add any companyId predicate to downstream queries. Layer 3 (prod DB): SELECT relrowsecurity,relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class JOIN pg_namespace WHERE nspname='axhy' → all 33 tables relrowsecurity=false; SELECT * FROM pg_policies WHERE schemaname='axhy' → 0 rows. Layer 4 (side-effect): the GUC is set on every write tx but no axhy-schema policy consumes current_setting('axhy.current_company_id') — confirmed by the empty policy set. Net: the 'defense in depth' described in route docs does not exist for tenant tables.
expected: Either (a) RLS policies enabled+FORCED on tenant tables filtering on current_setting('axhy.current_company_id') so the GUC actually backstops a forgotten app-layer filter, or (b) the misleading 'RLS fires as defense in depth' comments removed and replaced with an explicit 'app-layer filtering is the ONLY isolation; there is no DB backstop' warning so future authors do not assume a safety net that isn't there.
actual: GUC is written on every transaction but no axhy-schema RLS policy reads it; isolation is single-layer (app code only) while comments across the codebase assert a second RLS layer that does not exist.

title: Dormant legacy JWT auth mode trusts companyId from the token with ZERO DB verification when the 'epoch' claim is absent

So the legacy branch is unreachable by an attacker today. Layer 3 (DB): n/a — the risk is the absence of the membership check in this branch, not a data row.

actual: The legacy branch remains in place and would trust token-supplied companyId with no DB check for any no-epoch token; it is currently dormant only because such tokens have expired and cannot be forged, not because the unsafe code path was removed.

title: Chat leaks its Redis PROCESSING reservation on three early-return branches, locking the supervisor out of that message (409 IN_FLIGHT) for the full 120s TTL

evidence: LAYER 2 (route): chat.ts:637 reserveIdempotency sets __PROCESSING__ for 120s (chat-idempotency.ts:67-80, TTL_MS=120000). chat.ts:693-696 returns 503 CHAT_BUSY with NO releaseIdempotency call (it is before the try block at :698). chat.ts:700-706 returns AI_NOT_CONFIGURED inside the try, so it never reaches the catch block (:1408) where releaseIdempotency lives — only finally runs (releaseChatSlot). chat.ts:1413-1419 returns on AICostBudgetError inside the catch BEFORE the Promise.allSettled([recordCircuitFailure, releaseIdempotency]) at :1427. The irony: the comment at :1421-1424 states releaseIdempotency 'MUST still run — otherwise the supervisor is locked out of chat ... because the slot stays PROCESSING', yet the budget-exceeded branch above it bypasses exactly that. title: Idempotency cache ignores request body: a reused key with a DIFFERENT payload returns the stale cached response and silently drops the new request (no body-hash on either implementation)

scenario: A client reuses an Idempotency-Key it already used for a DIFFERENT body — e.g. mobile generates one key per screen-session instead of per-action, or a developer copy-pastes a key. Chat: same key, a genuinely new message text. Complaints/invites: same key, edited content.
evidence: LAYER 2: checkIdempotencyKey (idempotency-key.ts:86-94) looks up only the composite (companyId, routeKey, idempotencyKey) and returns row.responseJson — the request body is never read or hashed. withIdempotency (:185-189) returns the cached body and skips handler() entirely. LAYER 3 (DB): the IdempotencyKey table (verified columns: companyId, routeKey, idempotencyKey, responseStatus, responseJson, createdAt, expiresAt) has NO request-hash column, so detecting a payload mismatch is impossible. title: Clock-in write has no from-state guard: a CANCELLED (terminal, billable) visit can be resurrected to IN_PROGRESS via a clock-in racing a supervisor cancel
where: apps/backend/src/lib/services/worker-lifecycle-service.ts:92-118 (clockInVisit); legal edges in packages/state-machines/src/visit.ts:143-147 (CANCELLED has only ARCHIVE_THRESHOLD_REACHED; no edge to IN_PROGRESS)
scenario: A visit is SCHEDULED/NOTIFIED. The worker taps Start (clock-in) at the same moment a supervisor cancels the visit. clockInVisit reads state=SCHEDULED and passes the CLOCK_IN_LEGAL_FROM JS check; meanwhile the cancel commits, moving the row to CANCELLED; then clock-in's unconditional `update({ where:{ id } })` overwrites it to IN_PROGRESS.
evidence: LAYER 2 code: the from-state is validated only against the stale JS snapshot (line 92 `if (!CLOCK_IN_LEGAL_FROM.includes(visit.state))`), but the actual write at line 112-118 is `tx.visit.update({ where:{ id: visitId }, data:{ state:'IN_PROGRESS' } })` with no `state` in the WHERE, so it cannot detect the row moved to CANCELLED. LAYER 3 DB (prod): interleaved two-client transaction — clock-in read returned state=SCHEDULED ('passes CLOCK_IN_LEGAL_FROM'); a concurrent client committed `UPDATE Visit SET state='CANCELLED' WHERE id=.. AND state='SCHEDULED'` (cancel committed); then the clock-in client committed its unconditional UPDATE. Final prod-DB read: state='IN_PROGRESS'. CANCELLED→IN_PROGRESS is not an edge in visit.ts. LAYER 4: CANCELLED is in BILLABLE_VISIT_STATES (visit.ts:167-173); resurrecting it to IN_PROGRESS double-counts the work and lets it re-enter capture/submit/AI-verify, producing a second billable terminal state for the same scheduled visit. actual: The clock-in unconditionally forces state='IN_PROGRESS' regardless of the row's real current state, so a cancelled (or otherwise concluded) visit is silently revived into the active worker flow — an illegal transition the visit machine forbids.
